findings.headline: Treasury operations generated £0.231m net interest income despite the new £8m borrowing, outperforming expectations
findings.detail: The council managed its cash to generate returns while funding capital investment. Although it anticipated that net interest costs would be required in 2025/26, it actually achieved net interest income of £0.231m at an average portfolio return of 3.71%. The Ratio of Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream improved from -2.29% to -0.98%, both negative figures indicating net interest income rather than cost.
findings.matters: Shows the council has active, competent treasury management that generated positive returns while funding capital needs, enhancing the council's financial position despite taking on new debt.
findings.figures: Interest income £0.231m; average investment return 3.71%; average investment size £1.647m; Financing Costs ratio -0.98%
findings.quote: No target was set for 2025/26 as it was assumed that a net interest payable amount would be required to meet the Council's capital programme. Actual interest income from interest activity amounted to £0.231m.

findings.headline: Council took on £8m new debt in 2025/26, shifting from a net cash position to net borrowing
findings.detail: The council had zero external debt at the end of 2024/25 but borrowed £8m during 2025/26 at an average rate of 5.4%. This borrowing was within the approved Operational Boundary of £80m and represented the first time the council has used external borrowing in recent years.
findings.matters: A material change in the council's debt position is a significant financial decision that a lender would need to understand in terms of the council's capital programme, debt sustainability, and capacity to service new obligations.
findings.figures: Total Debt increased from £0 (2024/25) to £8m (2025/26); average rate 5.4%; Operational Boundary £80m; used 10% of limit

findings.headline: Regeneration scheme contract management was not operational at audit time; now being monitored with independent quantity surveyor
findings.detail: Ryecroft, Midway Car Park and Astley Place regeneration schemes had planned but not yet operational client-side contract management at audit time. High priority recommendation raised. Now arrangements in place using check/challenge meetings, formal progress meetings, draw down schedules, and independent quantity surveyor to value and certify works against contract value.
findings.matters: Capital schemes with weak initial governance pose risk of overspend or developer non-performance; follow-up assurance has been added to 2026-27 plan
findings.figures: One high priority recommendation; three schemes affected (Ryecroft, Midway Car Park, Astley Place)
findings.quote: Client-side contract management arrangements for the Ryecroft, Midway Car Park and Astley Place regeneration schemes was made. At the time of audit, key arrangements for oversight of the build phase were planned but not yet operational.

findings.headline: No formal approval process for homelessness service credit card spending; historically given verbally only
findings.detail: High priority finding on Homelessness and Rough Sleepers Grants: credit card expenditure was approved verbally with no documented audit trail. No assurance that purchases were appropriate, authorised, or linked to assessed client need. Now documented formal approval process in place with transactions reviewed before or after spend.
findings.matters: Absence of documented approval for public spending weakens assurance on proper use of funds; risk of improper expenditure was present
findings.figures: One high priority recommendation; now implemented
findings.quote: A high priority recommendation was raised as no formal process was in place for approving credit card expenditure, with approvals given verbally and no documented audit trail retained. This weakened assurance that purchases were appropriate, authorised and linked to assessed client need, increasing the risk of improper use of public funds.

findings.headline: Multiple financial systems lack documented policies and rely on manual processes without independent review
findings.detail: Recurring theme across E-Payments, Accounts Receivable, and others: key processes not clearly documented, policies not reviewed recently (Accounts Receivable policy not updated since 2023), manual reconciliations performed without independent review, and insufficient audit trails. E-Payments and Main Accounting both have manual reconciliations with no independent check.
findings.matters: Undocumented and manual processes are prone to error and harder to audit; lack of independent review means errors or fraud could persist
findings.figures: Multiple systems in draft or with Adequate Assurance; Accounts Receivable policy last reviewed 2023
findings.quote: In a number of areas, arrangements were operating in practice but were not fully documented, formally approved, version controlled or kept up to date.

findings.headline: Capacity and resourcing pressures explicitly constraining control effectiveness across multiple functions
findings.detail: The audit identifies capacity and resourcing as a cross-cutting theme affecting control consistency. Accounts Receivable reconciliations were not completed for a period due to resourcing pressures. Supported Accommodation implementation was delayed due to capacity. Audit staff turnover meant audits were reallocated and delayed; Service Director for Legal and Governance departure caused further delays.
findings.matters: A council facing sustained capacity constraints cannot reliably operate its financial controls; this is a structural risk rather than a single fixable issue
findings.figures: Audit work 'indicated' capacity pressures in 'some areas'; two audits not completed due to staff turnover and timing; Senior Audit Manager directing work through service agreement with Staffordshire County Council (341 days delivered)
findings.quote: Audit work also indicated that, in some areas, capacity and resourcing pressures were affecting the consistency with which controls could be operated or followed through in practice.

findings.headline: Debt recovery is not progressing in timely manner with delays in enforcement and prolonged case inactivity
findings.detail: Accounts Receivable audit found debt recovery activity delayed with inadequate escalation and enforcement. Cases remain inactive for extended periods and debts are not being advanced to appropriate enforcement stages. Management is implementing automated scheduling of recovery action, but the audit found limited visibility due to reliance on manual spreadsheets with no independent review.
findings.matters: Slow debt recovery directly affects cash collection and council liquidity; weak oversight means money owed is not being pursued effectively
findings.figures: Accounts Receivable given Adequate Assurance (Draft); one high priority recommendation on debt recovery process
findings.quote: Debt recovery activity is not being progressed in a timely and controlled manner, with delays in reminder and escalation actions, prolonged inactivity on cases, and debts not being advanced to appropriate enforcement stages where recovery remains outstanding.

findings.headline: Payroll control weaknesses including shared admin accounts and users approving their own changes
findings.detail: The payroll audit resulted in Limited Assurance due to three high priority issues: shared administrator accounts used by multiple officers (preventing attribution of actions), lack of prompt access removal when staff leave relevant roles, and inadequate segregation of duties allowing users to submit and approve their own payroll amendments including changes to their own records. Management is liaising with Stoke-on-Trent City Council (payroll provider) to issue individual accounts.
findings.matters: Weak controls over payroll processing create fraud risk and reduce accountability; the council cannot currently audit who made what change to payroll records
findings.figures: Three high priority recommendations; one additional security-related recommendation withheld
findings.quote: Collectively, these weaknesses increased the risk of unauthorised or inappropriate changes to payroll records, fraud, error and reduced accountability, and were a key factor in the limited assurance opinion for this review.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budgets and Strategies 2026-27, FEBRUARY 2026 - Council
findings.headline: Future budget stability dependent on non-recurring funding sources: Recovery Grant (£398-500k) and Extended Producer Responsibility (£274k).
findings.detail: The council is using Recovery Grant funding of £398k in 2027/28 and £500k in 2028/29 to offset settlement reductions, explicitly to 'smooth the impact of the Fair Funding Review 2.0'. Additionally, Extended Producer Responsibility income (£274k) is being used to fund 2026/27 savings. Neither source is permanent government funding, and the Recovery Grant is explicitly temporary smoothing of a structural funding cliff.
findings.matters: Using temporary grants and non-base revenue to plug structural deficits defers but does not solve underlying financial problems. When Recovery Grant expires after 2028/29, the council will face further unbudgeted gaps unless additional permanent savings are identified, suggesting the 2030/31 funding gap may be understated.
findings.figures: Recovery Grant 2027/28: £398k, 2028/29: £500k (both identified as temporary smoothing); Extended Producer Responsibility 2026/27: £274k
findings.quote: The increase in the minimum level will be financed from the Recovery Grant to be received in 2026/27, the balance of which will be paid into the Budget and Borrowing Support Fund to increase the Council's financial resilience, ahead of its use in 2027/28 and 2028/29 to smooth the impact of the Fair Funding Review 2.0.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budgets and Strategies 2026-27, FEBRUARY 2026 - Council
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement growing to £31.279m by 2028/29 dependent on three regeneration projects delivering forecast capital receipts.
findings.detail: The council is pursuing a £110m capital programme over 2026/27-2028/29, with Capital Financing Requirement growing 57% from £19.893m (March 2025) to £31.279m (March 2029). Three major schemes—York Place (£13.451m), Midway Carpark (£32.237m), and Ryecroft (£29.078m)—dominate the programme. Crucially, interest is being capitalised on these schemes based on assumptions they will generate capital receipts. Slippage or underperformance in receipt realisations would increase revenue debt servicing costs.
findings.matters: A lender tracks debt trajectory and the assumptions underlying capital strategies. Betting on capital receipts from three concurrent regeneration schemes that have not yet delivered creates execution risk. Failed or delayed receipts would force revenue budget to absorb capitalised interest costs.
findings.figures: CFR at 31/3/25: £19.893m; forecast at 31/3/29: £31.279m (57% growth); York Place capitalised interest, Midway capitalised interest, Ryecroft capitalised interest all dependent on receipt realisation
findings.quote: The Capital Programme for 2026/27 to 2028/29 includes an estimate for the development of York Place, which has been updated to reflect an adjusted cashflow and receipt of Homes England funding (£5.076m), this assumes spend of £13.451m plus capitalised interest over the period 2026/27 to 2027/28 and a subsequent capital receipt including capitalised interest during 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budgets and Strategies 2026-27, FEBRUARY 2026 - Council
findings.headline: Unresolved funding gaps in MTFS beyond 2026/27, with 2030/31 showing £365k residual gap after all identified savings.
findings.detail: While 2026/27 budget is balanced, the 5-year MTFS shows only partial solutions to future deficits. After savings of £560k are applied in 2030/31, a gap of £365k remains unfunded. Additionally, potential loss of recycling credits (£195k in 2027/28, £250k in 2028/29) if the County Council takes contractor disposal is flagged as a material risk.
findings.matters: A residual funding gap in the final year of the MTFS indicates either the savings plan is incomplete or further service reductions will be needed. Lenders assess councils on whether they have credible multi-year financial plans; unresolved deficits in the outer years are a warning sign.
findings.figures: 2030/31 remaining gap £365k after £560k identified savings; potential recycling income loss £195k (2027/28) and £250k (2028/29)
findings.quote: The MTFS indicates a budget shortfall of £1.599m for 2026/27, further years funding gaps are shown on the table below and in further detail at Appendix 5.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budgets and Strategies 2026-27, FEBRUARY 2026 - Council
findings.headline: Household waste service forecast to overspend by £0.275m in 2025/26 due to agency staffing and contractor costs.
findings.detail: Overtime, casual and agency staffing within Household Waste and Food Waste Services, combined with increased contractor disposal payments, has created an overspend of £0.206m at quarter three, forecast to reach £0.275m for the full year. This represents a structural cost pressure in what should be a controlled statutory service.
findings.matters: Inability to control costs in a core statutory waste service through labour market pressures and contractor pricing suggests the council faces systemic cost inflation that may affect other services. Forecasting accuracy is also at risk if in-year variances are this large.
findings.figures: £0.206m actual at Q3, £0.275m forecast full year overspend
findings.quote: Use of overtime, casual and agency staff within the Household Waste and Food Waste Services along with increased contractor disposal payments has resulted in an overspend of £0.206m at the close of quarter three. It is forecast that this will amount to an overspend of £0.275m for the financial year.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budgets and Strategies 2026-27, FEBRUARY 2026 - Council
findings.headline: Business Rates Collection Fund deficit of £1.193m due to successful property appeals creating reserve drawdown.
findings.detail: The council faces a Business Rates Collection Fund deficit estimated at £2.982m across all preceptors for 2025/26, of which the council's share is £1.193m. This results from successful property appeals in January-March 2025, creating an adverse variance of £2.291m from the December 2024 forecast. The deficit will be covered by drawdown from Business Rates Reserve.
findings.matters: Material reserve drawdown to cover appeal-driven funding volatility demonstrates significant valuation risk in business rates income. Reserves are being depleted to manage volatility rather than accumulated as resilience buffer.
findings.figures: Collection fund deficit £2.982m (council share £1.193m); variance from forecast £2.291m adverse
findings.quote: The Business Rates Collection Fund is estimated to be in a deficit position at the close of 2025/26. The deficit is estimated to amount to £2.982m, of which the Council's share is £1.193m.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budgets and Strategies 2026-27, FEBRUARY 2026 - Council
findings.headline: Multiple revenue streams underperforming in 2025/26, with income shortfalls forecast to continue affecting cashflow.
findings.detail: Car parking, bereavement services, leisure memberships (pool closure), trade waste and land charges are all recording income significantly below budget in quarter three 2025/26. These shortfalls are forecast to total £0.504m for the full year (excluding the pool closure which is £0.254m additional). This suggests structural rather than temporary weakness in discretionary income sources.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the stability of a council's cash-generating services. Simultaneous underperformance across multiple unrelated revenue streams (parking, leisure, bereavement, waste) suggests market weakness or demand issues, not one-off problems.
findings.figures: Car parking £0.137m, trade waste £0.075m, bereavement services £0.176m, pool closure £0.254m forecast full year impact
findings.quote: Income shortfalls at the close of quarter three from car parking (£0.137m), trade waste (£0.075m), land charges (£0.044m) and bereavement services (£0.176m). It is forecast that these will total £0.504m for the financial year.

findings.headline: Authorised borrowing limit being increased from £75m to £170m, more than doubling the legal ceiling on external debt
findings.detail: The council is seeking Full Council approval to increase the maximum permitted borrowing from £75m (2025/26) to £170m (2028/29). This 127% increase in four years signals a strategic shift from reserve-funded to debt-funded capital investment.
findings.matters: Doubling the authorised borrowing limit requires explicit Council approval and signals that the council intends to move substantially into debt financing; it indicates both need and increased financial risk appetite
findings.quote: The Council is asked to approve the following authorised limit: Debt 75,000 [2025/26] 120,000 [2026/27] 145,000 [2027/28] 170,000 [2028/29]

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement growing 57% over four years, from £19.9m to £31.3m by 2028/29
findings.detail: The CFR—the underlying borrowing need—will rise from £19.893m (31 March 2025) to £31.279m (31 March 2029). This substantial increase represents the council's structural reliance on debt to fund the capital programme.
findings.matters: A rising CFR signals increasing structural debt; prudential regulation requires it to remain below the authorised limit and lenders track this trend as a measure of financial stress
findings.quote: The Capital Financing Requirement is set to increase to £31.279m by 2028/29 based on the 3-year Capital Programme for 2026/27 to 2028/29, the Capital Financing Requirement at 31 March 2025 (£19.893m)

findings.headline: Borrowing costs rising to £2.1m/year by 2035/36, totalling £16.2m over ten years and consuming growing share of revenue budget
findings.detail: Minimum revenue provision and interest payments will cost the revenue budget £16.2m over ten years, rising from £1.04m in 2026/27 to £2.11m by 2035/36. The ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream will rise from 4.80% to 6.33% by 2028/29, indicating increasing pressure on day-to-day spending.
findings.matters: Capital borrowing is not free; the council's revenue budget will bear increasing annual costs that reduce funds available for other services, and the trend worsens into the 2030s
findings.quote: The costs to the revenue budget relating to minimum revenue provision and interest payable on borrowings will be around £16.163m over 10 years, with the costs in each year 2026/27 to 2035/36 being as shown below

findings.headline: Regeneration projects worth £70m+ depend on asset sales from 2028/29 onwards that may not materialise on schedule
findings.detail: Regeneration spending peaks at £53.8m in 2026/27 and £23m in 2027/28, initially funded by 'regeneration borrowing.' The strategy assumes capital receipts will emerge from 2028/29 (£13.4m), 2029/30 (£27.3m), and 2030/31 (£32.7m) to service this debt. If asset sales fail or are delayed, the borrowing remains outstanding.
findings.matters: A material portion of the capital programme is predicated on disposing of regenerated assets within specific timescales; delayed sales extend the borrowing period and increase financing costs
findings.figures: Regeneration borrowing: £47.2m (2026/27), £23m (2027/28); Regeneration receipts expected: £13.4m (2028/29), £27.3m (2029/30), £32.7m (2030/31)
findings.quote: The Capital Programme will require to be financed by borrowing, primarily for cash flow purposes, whilst assets are procured and constructed, after which time significant capital receipts are expected.

findings.headline: £142.3m capital programme cannot be funded from capital receipts alone; significant borrowing is required
findings.detail: Over 2026/27 to 2035/36, capital expenditure totals £142.3m. The council explicitly states there will be insufficient receipts to meet all costs, creating a structural funding gap that must be met through borrowing across the entire decade.
findings.matters: Planned capital investment far exceeds available receipts, forcing the council into structural debt financing and reducing financial flexibility
findings.figures: £142.3m capital programme; £21.4m from capital receipts (15%); £11.5m from borrowing; remainder from external contributions and expected regeneration receipts
findings.quote: There will be insufficient capital receipts arising from planned sales to meet all the costs of the investment programme.

findings.headline: Right to Buy capital receipts have collapsed from a historically major funding source to £0.5m per annum
findings.detail: The council previously relied heavily on capital receipts from Aspire Housing Right to Buy sales. The strategy states these have 'diminished from historically high levels, both because of the present depressed property market and there being fewer potential purchasers as time goes by.' This substantially reduces the council's self-funding capacity for capital investment.
findings.matters: A major revenue stream that funded capital investment has effectively dried up, forcing reliance on borrowing and asset sales instead
findings.figures: Future Right to Buy sales income projected at £0.5m per annum
findings.quote: However, Right to Buy sales have diminished from historically high levels, both because of the present depressed property market and there being fewer potential purchasers as time goes by. Future sales income is projected to be in the range of £0.5m per annum.

findings.headline: Council holds £2.007m in general reserves specifically to cover investment property income shortfalls
findings.detail: The council has set aside this amount as a contingency against the possibility of net shortfalls from its commercial property investments. This reflects management's assessment that volatility in this revenue source is material enough to require dedicated reserve cover.
findings.matters: The size of the reserve relative to budget swing shows management views investment property income risk as material and real
findings.figures: £2.007m held in General Fund balances
findings.quote: A total of £2.007m is currently held in balances to cover this and other risks and can be drawn upon in the event of risks materialising.

findings.headline: Council's budget depends on returns from a commercial property portfolio that has made losses in three of the past four years
findings.detail: The council explicitly states it is dependent on commercial property rental income to achieve a balanced revenue budget. Yet the portfolio returned losses of £36k (2022/23), £142k (2023/24), and £93k (2024/25), before projecting a £122k profit for 2025/26. This shows material volatility in a revenue stream the council has declared essential.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council's budget stability rests on a volatile asset class, and whether the recent recovery will hold
findings.figures: 2022/23 £36k loss, 2023/24 £142k loss, 2024/25 £93k loss, 2025/26 £122k profit (estimate), 2026/27 £125k profit (estimate)
findings.quote: The Council is dependent on a return from investment property activity in terms of rentals to achieve a balanced revenue budget.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement growing £7.4m (37%) over three years from capital programme that is not fully resourced
findings.detail: CFR rises from £19.9m (31 March 2025 actual) to £32.3m (31 March 2028 forecast), a 62% increase. The strategy notes the council 'may therefore be required to borrow over the forecast period' and that it 'expects to comply' with CIPFA's Prudential Code recommendation that total debt be lower than highest forecast CFR. The implication is that existing resources are insufficient and borrowing is necessary.
findings.matters: Growing CFR means the council's capital ambition is expanding faster than its internal resources can fund; understanding what is driving this capital spend is essential.
findings.quote: The Council has an increasing CFR due to the capital programme and may therefore be required to borrow over the forecast period.

findings.headline: Interest rate forecast depends on November 2025 Budget and assumes Bank Rate falls to 3.75%, but risks are both up and down
findings.detail: Arlingclose forecast (dated 10 November 2024) assumes Bank Rate reaching 3.75% and holding there through 2026-28. However, the strategy explicitly notes this was issued before the November 2025 Budget and 'is likely to be revised'. The forecast shows material downside risks (Bank Rate could fall to 2.75% or lower) but also upside risks to yields. The council's strategy to borrow short-term now and long-term later depends on long-term rates falling or at least not rising sharply.
findings.matters: If the Budget or subsequent economic data shift the interest rate outlook, the council's borrowing costs and refinancing plans could change materially.
findings.figures: Arlingclose central case: Bank Rate 3.75% (from Dec-25 through Sep-28); downside risk: -1.00% (Bank Rate could reach 2.75%); 10-yr gilt yield forecast 4.40% with downside risk of -1.10%; Debt interest budget 2026-27: £738,780
findings.quote: This forecast was issued ahead of the Autumn Budget and is likely to be revised once the fiscal measures are announced on 26th November 2025 and their market implications are assessed.

findings.headline: Council deferring external borrowing by drawing on reserves and internal resources rather than taking long-term debt now
findings.detail: The strategy is explicit: maintain internal borrowing (using reserves and cash) rather than external debt, switching to external long-term borrowing only when interest rates are favorable. Currently holding £8.93m invested while forecasting need to borrow. Usable reserves forecast to remain between £9.9m and £10.6m across the period, providing the buffer for this strategy.
findings.matters: This defers certainty of financing costs but creates refinancing risk if long-term rates don't fall as expected or if the council needs cash sooner than planned.
findings.figures: Treasury investments held: £8.93m (14 Jan 2026); Usable reserves: £10.6m (2026), £9.9m (2027), £10.0m (2028-2029); Budget for investment income 2026-27: nil
findings.quote: The Council's current strategy is to maintain borrowing and investments below their underlying levels, sometimes known as internal borrowing. Where borrowing is required, this will be in line with Arlingclose's current advice of doing so from other local authorities on a short-term basis. This will be undertaken until it becomes advantageous to switch to long term debt, with the lowest cost option being considered.

findings.headline: Borrowing strategy dependent on capital receipts from regeneration projects not arriving until 2028-29
findings.detail: The forecast assumes capital receipts will materialise from regeneration projects starting in 2028-29, after which net loans requirement is forecast to fall from £87.6m to £73.3m by 2029. The council is currently using internal resources (reserves and working capital) to delay external borrowing, but if regeneration receipts are delayed or fall short, the refinancing risk and debt burden could be substantially worse.
findings.matters: Regeneration projects are discretionary and timings are uncertain; a lender needs to know what happens to cash flow and debt if expected receipts don't materialise.
findings.figures: Forecast net loans requirement falls from £87.6m (2028) to £73.3m (2029), an assumption built on capital receipts 'expected from 2028/29 onwards'; current working capital forecast shows swing from negative £9.3m (2026) through positive £65.3m (2028) to positive £52.0m (2029)
findings.quote: borrowing relating to regeneration projects, for which capital receipts are expected from 2028/29 onwards

findings.headline: External borrowing forecast to escalate sharply from zero to £87.6m by 2028-29 driven by capital expansion
findings.detail: The council currently holds no external borrowing but the liability benchmark forecasts net loans requirement of £7.5m in 2026, jumping to £61.3m by 2027 and peaking at £87.6m by 2028. This represents a fundamental shift from the council's current position as a net investor (£8.93m held 14 January 2026) to substantial external borrowing. The underlying driver is the Capital Financing Requirement growing from £27.4m to £32.3m over the period.
findings.matters: A council moving from holding cash to taking on £87.6m of debt signals major capital commitments ahead, and a lender needs to understand both the projects being funded and the council's ability to service that debt.
findings.figures: External borrowing forecast: £7.5m (2026), £61.3m (2027), £87.6m (2028); CFR: £27.4m (2026), £29.0m (2027), £32.3m (2028); Current holdings: £0 external borrowing, £8.93m investments
findings.quote: The balance sheet forecasts, in the table above, shows that the Council expects to borrow in 2026/27, in addition to undertaking borrowing towards the backend of the current year.

findings.headline: Castle Car Park £12m capital investment now operational and valued using investment method based on income forecasts, introducing new estimation risk
findings.detail: The council completed construction of the Castle Car Park at £12m during 2024/25 and reclassified it from Asset Under Construction to operational land and buildings. It is being valued at existing use value using the investment method, which depends on forecasted rental income and yield assumptions. This introduces new estimation uncertainty as the valuation relies entirely on assumptions about income-generation potential.
findings.matters: Material capital investment now depends on commercial income forecasts; if rental income underperforms assumptions, both valuation and recoverable asset value are at risk; signals council pursuing revenue-generation strategies dependent on market performance.
findings.figures: £12m capital cost; reclassified from AUC to operational; land and buildings balance sheet movement £2.2m (primarily this reclassification)
findings.quote: However, during the year, the Council has completed the construction of the Castle Car Park at a cost of £12m. This will be valued at its existing use value (EUV) using the investment method (based on its income potential).

findings.headline: Valuation working papers for significant assets contained formula errors and lacked formal management review of key assumptions
findings.detail: The auditors identified formula errors in the working papers supporting valuation of two specific assets. Additionally, data inputs provided by finance (e.g. cashflows) were not appropriately applied to elements of calculations, evidencing lack of management review. An absence of formal control reviewing assumptions adopted by valuers was noted, which directly responds to the significant audit risk over land and buildings valuation.
findings.matters: Material asset valuations (land and buildings £43.2m at prior year-end, £37.6m valued at depreciated replacement cost) are unreliable without proper review controls; directly increases risk of misstated balance sheet values.
findings.figures: Land and buildings £43.2m (prior year); £37.6m valued at DRC; investment property portfolio £13.5m (prior year)
findings.quote: On receipt of the workings to support the valuation of two specific assets, we identified formula errors for key assumptions in the valuation. Similarly, relevant data inputs had been provided by finance (e.g cashflows) which had not been appropriately applied to elements of the workings evidencing a lack of review by management over the valuation workings.

findings.headline: Pension asset valuation contained £885k uncorrected misstatement driven by actuary's return assumptions diverging significantly from actual
findings.detail: The council's IAS 19 actuarial valuation required revision from the initial 25 April 2025 report to a revised 23 May 2025 report after variances with actual benefits paid and contributions exceeded acceptable thresholds. The auditors identified a £885k uncorrected misstatement in pension assets, primarily because the actuary's estimated return rate diverged materially from actual administrator returns. This includes a £293k prior year misstatement that was not corrected.
findings.matters: Pension liabilities are material to council balance sheet (£137.6m); audit uncertainty about valuation methodology and actuary assumptions indicates control gap; uncorrected misstatements accumulating across years.
findings.figures: £885k uncorrected misstatement in 2024/25 (£293k prior year unadjusted); pension obligation £137.6m (down £22.1m year-on-year); pension assets £176.1m (up £2.6m)
findings.quote: This misstatement is driven by the differences between actual returns and those estimated by the actuary. This includes a £293k prior year misstatement that was uncorrected.

findings.headline: Capital programme underperformance continues: £25.1m underspent against £51.3m revised budget in 2024/25, following £44m underspend in 2023/24
findings.detail: The council began the year with a £59.9m capital programme of which £42.2m was delayed expenditure from 2023/24 when only 21% of budget was spent due to inflationary pressures. After mid-year review, the revised programme totalled £51.295m but actual expenditure reached only £26.3m. The auditors flag this persistent pattern as raising a 'risk that the Council loses credibility over its ability to forecast and progress schemes effectively' and recommend more robust challenge and monitoring with clear communication of slippage.
findings.matters: Persistent capital underspend signals forecasting weakness and delivery risk on council priorities; for lenders, unreliable project forecasting and execution capability poses risk to cashflow and asset deployment.
findings.figures: £59.9m initial programme; £51.295m revised programme; £26.3m actual spend (£25.1m below plan); prior year £44m underspend from 21% budget execution rate
findings.quote: following multiple years of delayed delivery, there is a risk that the Council loses credibility over its ability to forecast and progress schemes effectively

news_drafts.headline: Treasury operations generated £0.231m net interest income despite the new £8m borrowing, outperforming expectations
news_drafts.lead: Shows the council has active, competent treasury management that generated positive returns while funding capital needs, enhancing the council's financial position despite taking on new debt.

news_drafts.headline: Council took on £8m new debt in 2025/26, shifting from a net cash position to net borrowing
news_drafts.lead: A material change in the council's debt position is a significant financial decision that a lender would need to understand in terms of the council's capital programme, debt sustainability, and capacity to service new obligations.

news_drafts.headline: Regeneration scheme contract management was not operational at audit time; now being monitored with independent quantity surveyor
news_drafts.lead: Capital schemes with weak initial governance pose risk of overspend or developer non-performance; follow-up assurance has been added to 2026-27 plan
